hypotheses.title: SurplusGuildMinter.getRewards reads userStake before assignment
hypotheses.description: In `getRewards`, the code checks `if (lastGaugeLoss > uint256(userStake.lastGaugeLoss))` BEFORE `userStake = _stakes[user][term]` is assigned. At that point `userStake` is the default zero-value struct, so `userStake.lastGaugeLoss` is 0. This means the slashed flag is set to true whenever `lastGaugeLoss > 0`, regardless of whether the user actually has an unapplied loss. The subsequent `if (userStake.stakeTime == 0) return` uses the freshly-loaded stake, but the slashed determination is already wrong.
hypotheses.attackPath: After any gauge loss is ever notified (lastGaugeLoss > 0), any user calling `getRewards` (directly or via stake/unstake) will be incorrectly flagged as slashed. Their stake is wiped to zero and their CREDIT contribution to the surplus buffer is forfeited, even if they had already applied the loss or staked after the loss.
hypotheses.impact: Users lose their staked CREDIT and GUILD positions incorrectly; surplus buffer accounting is corrupted; users cannot unstake.
hypotheses.recommendation: Move `userStake = _stakes[user][term];` before the `lastGaugeLoss` comparison.

hypotheses.title: LendingTerm.initialize uses assert instead of require, bricking proxy
hypotheses.description: The initialize function uses `assert(address(core()) == address(0))` to guard against re-initialization. In Solidity 0.8.x, a failing assert consumes all gas and reverts. More importantly, the constructor sets `_core = Core(address(1))`, so `address(core())` is `address(1)`, not `address(0)`. This means the assert will ALWAYS fail on a freshly cloned proxy, making initialize() permanently revert and the term unusable.
hypotheses.attackPath: Any user calling `LendingTermOnboarding.createTerm()` will have the clone's initialize() revert because `core()` returns address(1) (set in constructor), not address(0). The assert `address(core()) == address(0)` fails, consuming all gas. No term can ever be created.
hypotheses.impact: Complete denial of service for term creation; the entire onboarding flow is broken. No lending terms can be deployed.
hypotheses.recommendation: Change the constructor to set `_core = address(0)` (or use a dedicated `initialized` flag), and replace `assert` with `require` with a descriptive message.

hypotheses.title: LendingTerm.onBid allows bidder to receive collateral without full debt repayment
hypotheses.description: In `onBid`, if `creditFromBidder < principal`, the code sets `pnl = creditFromBidder - principal` (negative), sets `principal = creditFromBidder`, and requires `collateralToBorrower == 0`. This means the bidder pays less than the principal and receives ALL the collateral (`collateralToBidder = collateralAmount`). The protocol records a loss equal to the shortfall. This is by design for auctions, but the issue is that `AuctionHouse.getBidDetail` in the second phase linearly decreases `creditAsked` to 0, so a bidder can wait until near the end and pay a tiny amount for the full collateral, sticking the protocol with the loss. The auction mechanism is supposed to find a fair price, but with no minimum bid and a 30-minute window, a bidder can snipe at the last block for near-zero CREDIT.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker observes a called loan with valuable collateral. 2) Attacker waits until `block.timestamp` is just before `startTime + auctionDuration`. 3) Attacker calls `bid(loanId)`; `creditAsked` is near 0, `collateralReceived = collateralAmount`. 4) Attacker pays near-zero CREDIT, receives full collateral. 5) Protocol records full principal loss.
hypotheses.impact: Protocol absorbs bad debt; CREDIT holders diluted; attacker profits from collateral at near-zero cost.
hypotheses.recommendation: Enforce a minimum bid (e.g., a fraction of `callDebt`) or extend the auction if bids are too low.

hypotheses.title: AuctionHouse forgive() can be called by anyone, forcing bad debt on protocol
hypotheses.description: `forgive(bytes32 loanId)` is callable by anyone once `creditAsked == 0` (i.e., after the auction's second phase fully elapses). It calls `LendingTerm.onBid` with `creditFromBidder = 0`, which triggers `notifyPnL` with a negative PnL equal to the full principal. This is intended for frozen collateral, but any untrusted actor can call it as soon as the auction duration passes, even if a bidder would have bid at a nonzero price. More importantly, the auction's second phase linearly decreases `creditAsked` to 0; at the very end, `creditAsked == 0` and anyone can forgive, wiping the debt and leaving collateral stuck in the LendingTerm. The borrower keeps the CREDIT, the protocol eats the loss, and the collateral is stranded (only recoverable via governor `emergencyAction`).
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker observes a called loan whose auction is about to end. 2) Attacker waits until `block.timestamp >= startTime + auctionDuration`. 3) Attacker calls `AuctionHouse.forgive(loanId)`. 4) `onBid` is invoked with 0 credit, `notifyPnL` records full principal loss, `creditMultiplier` may drop, surplus buffer depleted. 5) Collateral remains in LendingTerm, borrower keeps CREDIT.
hypotheses.impact: Protocol absorbs full bad debt; CREDIT holders diluted; collateral stranded; borrower profits by keeping borrowed CREDIT without repaying.
hypotheses.recommendation: Require that `forgive` can only be called after a grace period AND that no bid was possible, or restrict `forgive` to governance/guardian role.

hypotheses.title: SurplusGuildMinter.unstake can be front-run by loss to avoid slashing
hypotheses.description: `unstake` calls `getRewards` which checks `lastGaugeLoss > userStake.lastGaugeLoss`. If a loss has occurred but `applyGaugeLoss` has not been called on the user, `getRewards` sets `slashed = true` and returns early in `unstake` (the `if (slashed) return;`). This means the user's stake is zeroed and their CREDIT is forfeited. However, a user can front-run a loss notification by calling `unstake` before `notifyGaugeLoss` is called. Since `notifyGaugeLoss` is called by ProfitManager during `notifyPnL`, and `notifyPnL` is called by the LendingTerm during `onBid` or `forgive`, a user monitoring the mempool can see the loss transaction and front-run with `unstake`, withdrawing their CREDIT before the loss is recorded. The `lastGaugeLoss` is only set when `notifyGaugeLoss` executes, so the front-running `unstake` sees no loss and succeeds.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker stakes CREDIT in a term via `SurplusGuildMinter.stake`. 2) Attacker monitors mempool for a transaction that will trigger a loss in that term (e.g., `AuctionHouse.forgive` or `bid` at low price). 3) Attacker front-runs with `unstake(term, fullAmount)`. 4) `getRewards` sees no loss yet, `unstake` succeeds, attacker withdraws CREDIT. 5) Loss occurs, but attacker's stake is already gone; they avoid slashing.
hypotheses.impact: Attacker avoids losing their CREDIT stake to the surplus buffer; protocol absorbs the loss; other stakers bear disproportionate burden.
hypotheses.recommendation: Implement a withdrawal delay or require that `unstake` checks for pending losses in the current block.

hypotheses.title: Offboarding cleanup can be permanently blocked by re-onboarding term
hypotheses.description: `cleanup()` requires `GuildToken(guildToken).isDeprecatedGauge(term)` to be true. However, `proposeOnboard()` in LendingTermOnboarding allows re-onboarding a previously offboarded term (it only checks `!isGauge(term)`, and `isGauge` returns false for deprecated gauges). If a term is re-onboarded via `addGauge`, `_addGauge` calls `_deprecatedGauges.remove(gauge)`, making `isDeprecatedGauge` return false. The `nOffboardingsInProgress` counter is never decremented, and PSM redemptions stay paused forever.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker triggers offboarding of term T (quorum met), `nOffboardingsInProgress` becomes 1 and PSM redemptions are paused. 2) Before `cleanup(T)` is called, attacker (or any GUILD holder) calls `proposeOnboard(T)` and passes the governance vote, re-adding T as a live gauge. 3) `cleanup(T)` now reverts on the `isDeprecatedGauge` check. 4) `nOffboardingsInProgress` stays at 1, so PSM redemptions remain paused indefinitely, and the term's roles are never revoked.
hypotheses.impact: PSM redemptions permanently frozen (CREDIT cannot be redeemed for peg token), term roles never cleaned up, protocol accounting stuck. Loss of peg stability and user funds trapped.
hypotheses.recommendation: Track offboardings per-term and allow cleanup regardless of re-onboarding, or block re-onboarding while an offboarding is in progress for that term.

hypotheses.title: ProfitManager gauge profit index not updated on loss, allowing stale reward claims
hypotheses.description: When a loss is notified (`amount < 0`), `notifyPnL` calls `GuildToken.notifyGaugeLoss(gauge)` but does NOT update `gaugeProfitIndex[gauge]`. Users who voted for the gauge can still call `claimGaugeRewards` and receive rewards based on the last profit index, even though the gauge just suffered a loss. The `GuildToken._decrementGaugeWeight` calls `claimGaugeRewards` before decrementing, so a user can claim pending rewards right before their weight is slashed. More critically, after a loss, the gauge's profit index remains at its pre-loss value, and any subsequent profit notification will compute `deltaIndex` from the stale index, potentially over-rewarding users who should have been slashed.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker votes for gauge G, accruing profit index. 2) A loss occurs in G (via a loan default). 3) Attacker calls `claimGaugeRewards` before `applyGaugeLoss` is called on them — receives full pending CREDIT rewards. 4) Attacker's GUILD weight is then slashed, but they already extracted rewards. 5) Alternatively, attacker waits for next profit in G; `gaugeProfitIndex` is still old, so `deltaIndex` includes the pre-loss period, over-rewarding.
hypotheses.impact: CREDIT rewards paid out to users whose gauge suffered a loss; surplus buffer depleted; CREDIT holders diluted.
hypotheses.recommendation: On loss notification, reset or adjust `gaugeProfitIndex[gauge]` to prevent stale reward claims, or require `applyGaugeLoss` before claiming.

hypotheses.title: LendingTerm.initialize can be front-run on cloned terms
hypotheses.description: `initialize()` has no access control and only asserts `address(core()) == address(0)`. The implementation contract sets core to address(1) in its constructor, but clones created via `Clones.clone` start with core == address(0). Between `createTerm` cloning and the factory's own `initialize` call, an attacker can call `initialize` on the clone with attacker-chosen refs/params. Even worse, the factory calls `initialize` in the same transaction, so the race is only within the same tx — but any clone deployed outside the factory (or a clone whose initialize reverts) is fully hijackable. More critically, the factory's `createTerm` is permissionless, so an attacker can call `createTerm` themselves and then immediately call `initialize` on the returned clone with malicious refs before the factory does — but the factory does it atomically. The real exposure: any clone that is not initialized by the factory (e.g., if `initialize` reverts on the factory path due to a bad param) remains open, and any clone deployed by a third party using the same implementation is fully attacker-controlled.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker observes a pending `createTerm` tx or deploys their own clone of an allowed implementation. 2) Attacker calls `initialize` with `_core` = attacker-controlled address, refs pointing to attacker contracts. 3) The clone now trusts attacker's core/refs; all subsequent borrow/repay/call flows route through attacker contracts.
hypotheses.impact: Full takeover of a LendingTerm clone: attacker can mint CREDIT via a fake creditMinter, drain collateral, or brick the term. Loss of funds for any user interacting with the hijacked term.
hypotheses.recommendation: Make `initialize` callable only by the factory (e.g., pass `msg.sender == deployer` check or use an `onlyFactory` modifier), or have the factory pass a one-time initialization token.

hypotheses.title: Partial repay lets borrower shrink principal without paying accrued interest
hypotheses.description: `_partialRepay` computes `percentRepaid = debtToRepay * 1e18 / loanDebt` where `loanDebt` includes accrued interest, then reduces `loan.borrowAmount` by `issuanceDecrease = borrowAmount * percentRepaid / 1e18`. Because `percentRepaid` is derived from the interest-inclusive debt, the principal reduction is larger than the fraction of principal actually repaid. The borrower pays `debtToRepay` (which is split into `principalRepaid` and `interestRepaid`), but the loan's stored `borrowAmount` shrinks by a larger amount than `principalRepaid`, so future interest accrues on a smaller principal than the borrower actually still owes.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Borrower opens a loan with a large interest rate. 2) Waits until interest has accrued so `loanDebt > borrowAmount`. 3) Calls `partialRepay` with the minimum allowed amount. 4) `percentRepaid` is computed against the inflated `loanDebt`, so `issuanceDecrease` (principal reduction) exceeds the actual principal portion paid. 5) Repeat each period; the borrower's effective principal decays faster than the CREDIT they actually paid, and the term's `issuance` accounting understates real debt.
hypotheses.impact: Borrowers systematically underpay interest; the term's `issuance` and `borrowAmount` drift below real outstanding debt, causing the protocol to under-collect interest and misreport debt ceilings. Over time this can lead to insolvency of the term and incorrect `totalBorrowedCredit` used for gauge ceilings.
hypotheses.recommendation: Compute `percentRepaid` against the principal portion only (or reduce `borrowAmount` by `principalRepaid * creditMultiplier / borrowCreditMultiplier`), so principal reduction matches the principal actually repaid.

hypotheses.title: AuctionHouse bid uses stale callDebt allowing underpayment after creditMultiplier drop
hypotheses.description: The auction's `callDebt` is snapshotted at call time in LendingTerm._call() and never refreshed. If the creditMultiplier decreases (bad debt elsewhere) during the auction, the loan's actual debt in CREDIT terms increases (getLoanDebt scales by borrowCreditMultiplier/creditMultiplier), but the auction still asks only the old `callDebt`. A bidder can pay the stale, lower amount and receive the full collateral, leaving the protocol with a shortfall that is silently absorbed as a loss.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker observes a loan called with callDebt D. 2) Attacker (or anyone) triggers a loss notification in another term via a legitimate path (e.g., a forgive() by governor is not needed — a normal auction loss on another term reduces creditMultiplier). 3) creditMultiplier drops, so the called loan's true debt is now D' > D. 4) Attacker bids in phase 2 paying only D (or less), receiving full collateral. 5) onBid computes principal using the new (lower) creditMultiplier, so creditFromBidder < principal, and the difference is booked as a loss to the surplus buffer / credit holders.
hypotheses.impact: Protocol takes bad debt; CREDIT holders and surplus buffer lose funds; attacker captures collateral at below-market cost.
hypotheses.recommendation: Recompute the loan debt at bid time (or cap the auction's creditAsked to the current getLoanDebt) so the auction always asks the up-to-date debt.

hypotheses.title: Reentrancy in LendingTerm.onBid via malicious collateral token
hypotheses.description: In `onBid`, the loan's `closeTime` is set and `issuance` is decremented before collateral is transferred to the borrower and bidder via `safeTransfer`. If the collateral token is a malicious ERC20 (or ERC-777) that calls back into the LendingTerm during the transfer, the attacker can re-enter `onBid` for the same loanId. The check `require(loans[loanId].closeTime == 0)` would block a second `onBid`, but the attacker can instead re-enter `_borrow`/`borrow` or `_call`/`call` on other loans, or re-enter `AuctionHouse.bid` for a different loan whose state was already mutated. More critically, the `AuctionHouse.bid` function decrements `nAuctionsInProgress` and sets `endTime` before calling `onBid`, so a reentrant call into `AuctionHouse.bid` for the same loanId would revert on `getBidDetail` (endTime != 0), but reentrancy into `LendingTerm.borrow` while `issuance` was just decremented allows borrowing against stale debt-ceiling accounting.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker deploys a malicious collateral token that reenters on transfer. 2) Attacker opens a loan, gets it called, and bids on the auction. 3) During `safeTransfer` of collateral to the attacker (bidder), the token's `transfer` hook reenters `LendingTerm.borrow` or `ProfitManager.notifyPnL`-adjacent flows. 4) Because `issuance` was already decremented and `closeTime` set, the attacker can borrow again with a debt ceiling that doesn't account for the just-closed loan, or manipulate `creditMultiplier` accounting.
hypotheses.impact: Incorrect debt-ceiling accounting, potential over-borrowing beyond gauge limits, and inconsistent `issuance`/`totalBorrowedCredit` state leading to protocol insolvency.
hypotheses.recommendation: Apply the checks-effects-interactions pattern strictly: perform all collateral transfers after all state updates and use a reentrancy guard on `onBid`, `_borrow`, `_repay`, `_partialRepay`, and `_call`.

hypotheses.title: Reverting collateral token blocks repay and traps borrower collateral
hypotheses.description: `_repay` ends with `IERC20(params.collateralToken).safeTransfer(loan.borrower, loan.collateralAmount)`. If the collateral token has a transfer hook, blacklist, or pause that reverts for the borrower (or globally), the entire `repay()` reverts. The borrower cannot repay to close the loan and recover collateral. The only escape is `forgive()` (governor-only) or `call()` + auction, but `onBid` also transfers collateral to borrower/bidder and can revert similarly. There is no borrower-accessible path to close the loan without a collateral transfer.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Borrower has a loan with a collateral token that blacklists the borrower (or the token is paused). 2) Borrower calls `repay()` — reverts on `safeTransfer`. 3) Borrower cannot close the loan; debt keeps accruing interest. 4) If the term is deprecated, `call()` triggers auction; `onBid` also reverts on collateral transfer, so the auction cannot conclude. 5) Funds are stuck until governor calls `forgive()`.
hypotheses.impact: Borrower's collateral and debt are stuck; interest accrues indefinitely; only governance can resolve. Loss of funds / frozen state.
hypotheses.recommendation: Allow repay to succeed even if collateral transfer fails (e.g., escrow collateral for later claim), or provide a borrower-accessible path to close the loan without transferring collateral.

hypotheses.title: LendingTermOffboarding supportOffboard uses getPastVotes at snapshotBlock — vote replay across polls
hypotheses.description: `supportOffboard(snapshotBlock, term)` reads `GuildToken.getPastVotes(msg.sender, snapshotBlock)`. A user's voting power at a given snapshotBlock can be used to support multiple polls for different terms at the same snapshotBlock, because `userPollVotes[msg.sender][snapshotBlock][term]` is keyed by term. This means a user with 1000 GUILD at block N can support offboarding of term A and term B simultaneously using the same 1000 votes. This is a double-voting issue: the same voting power is counted in multiple polls. While each poll is for a different term, the quorum for each poll is reached independently, so a single user's weight can push multiple terms over quorum. This is a known design choice in some systems, but here it allows a minority holder to offboard multiple terms.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker holds 1000 GUILD at block N. 2) Attacker calls supportOffboard(N, termA) and supportOffboard(N, termB) in the same block. 3) Both polls count 1000 weight from the attacker. 4) If quorum is 1000, both terms can be offboarded with the same voting power.
hypotheses.impact: A single holder can offboard multiple lending terms with the same voting power, potentially disrupting the protocol.
hypotheses.recommendation: Track total user weight used across all polls at a given snapshotBlock, or require a separate snapshot per poll.

hypotheses.title: Partial repay allows interest-only repayment to reset partial-repay timer
hypotheses.description: `_partialRepay` requires `principalRepaid != 0 && interestRepaid != 0` and `debtToRepay >= loanDebt * minPartialRepayPercent`. A borrower with a loan subject to `maxDelayBetweenPartialRepay` can make a minimal partial repay (just above `minPartialRepayPercent`) right before the delay expires, resetting `lastPartialRepay[loanId] = block.timestamp`. This lets the borrower indefinitely avoid being called, even if the loan is deeply underwater, by paying tiny amounts of interest. The `minPartialRepayPercent` is a per-repay minimum, not cumulative, so repeated tiny repays keep the loan alive.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Borrower opens loan with `maxDelayBetweenPartialRepay` set. 2) As delay approaches, borrower calls `partialRepay` with `debtToRepay = loanDebt * minPartialRepayPercent / 1e18` (minimum allowed). 3) `lastPartialRepay` resets, timer restarts. 4) Repeat indefinitely, keeping an underwater loan uncallable while collateral value drops.
hypotheses.impact: Lenders/CREDIT holders cannot call a bad loan; bad debt accumulates; protocol becomes insolvent if collateral value falls below debt.
hypotheses.recommendation: Track cumulative repayment since last reset, or require repayment of a percentage of the original principal, not just the current debt.

hypotheses.title: SurplusGuildMinter.stake can be used to inflate gauge weight and borrow against it
hypotheses.description: `stake` mints GUILD at `mintRatio` and increments the gauge weight. An attacker can stake a large amount of CREDIT, inflate the gauge weight, and borrow up to the inflated debt ceiling. The attacker's CREDIT is locked in the term's surplus buffer, but they can borrow more than they could otherwise. If the attacker defaults, the surplus buffer absorbs the loss, but the attacker keeps the borrowed CREDIT. This is a classic self-referential attack: stake to inflate ceiling, borrow, default, lose stake but keep borrowed funds. The net gain depends on `mintRatio` and the borrowed amount.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker acquires CREDIT (e.g., via PSM). 2) Attacker calls `SurplusGuildMinter.stake(term, largeAmount)`, minting GUILD and inflating gauge weight. 3) Attacker calls `LendingTerm.borrow` up to the new debt ceiling. 4) Attacker defaults (stops repaying). 5) Loan is called, auctioned; if collateral is insufficient, loss is recorded. 6) Attacker's stake is slashed, but they keep the borrowed CREDIT.
hypotheses.impact: Protocol absorbs bad debt; attacker profits if borrowed amount > staked amount.
hypotheses.recommendation: Cap the debt ceiling increase from SurplusGuildMinter stakes, or require a longer lock-up.

hypotheses.title: ERC20RebaseDistributor distribute() can be front-run to dilute new rebasers
hypotheses.description: `distribute(amount)` burns `amount` from `msg.sender` and increases the share price over `DISTRIBUTION_PERIOD`. A user can call `enterRebase()` right before a large `distribute` to capture a share of the distribution, then `exitRebase()` after the interpolation completes. Since `enterRebase` converts balance to shares at the current (pre-distribution) share price, the new rebaser gets shares at the old price and benefits from the full distribution. This is a classic rebase front-running attack. The `START_REBASING_SHARE_PRICE = 1e30` mitigates rounding but not the economic dilution. An attacker with a large balance can enter rebase just before a known distribution (e.g., from ProfitManager's `notifyPnL` profit path) and exit after, capturing a disproportionate share.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker monitors mempool for `notifyPnL` with positive amount (which calls `CreditToken.distribute`). 2) Attacker front-runs with `enterRebase()`. 3) Distribution occurs; share price increases over 30 days. 4) Attacker waits for interpolation to complete, calls `exitRebase()`, receiving a share of the distributed CREDIT. 5) Attacker exits, having captured rewards without holding CREDIT long-term.
hypotheses.impact: Long-term CREDIT holders receive diluted rewards; attacker extracts value from the savings rate mechanism.
hypotheses.recommendation: Require a minimum rebasing duration before rewards are claimable, or snapshot rebasing supply at distribution time.

hypotheses.title: AuctionHouse phase-1 collateral offer can be zero at start, allowing free collateral via rounding
hypotheses.description: In phase 1, `collateralReceived = collateralAmount * elapsed / midPoint`. At elapsed=0 (auction start block), this is 0, but `creditAsked = callDebt` (full debt). A bidder in the same block as startAuction would pay full debt for 0 collateral — not exploitable. However, the reverse: in phase 2, `creditAsked = callDebt - callDebt * elapsed / PHASE_2_DURATION`. Near the end, creditAsked can round to a very small non-zero value while collateralReceived = full collateralAmount, letting a bidder take all collateral for dust. The `require(creditAsked != 0)` only blocks exactly zero.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker waits until the last block before auctionDuration where creditAsked is still non-zero (e.g., 1 wei). 2) Calls bid(), paying 1 wei CREDIT for the entire collateral. 3) onBid sees creditFromBidder (1) < principal, books a large loss, and transfers full collateral to bidder.
hypotheses.impact: Attacker acquires collateral for ~0 cost; protocol books full principal as bad debt; credit holders lose.
hypotheses.recommendation: Enforce a minimum creditAsked (e.g., a fraction of callDebt) or require creditFromBidder to cover at least the principal before allowing full collateral transfer.

hypotheses.title: SurplusGuildMinter.getRewards reentrancy via CreditToken transfer
hypotheses.description: `getRewards` calls `ProfitManager(profitManager).claimRewards(address(this))` which transfers CREDIT to this contract, then computes `creditReward` and `guildReward`, and transfers them to the user via `CreditToken(credit).transfer(user, creditReward)` and `RateLimitedMinter(rlgm).mint(user, guildReward)`. The state update `_stakes[user][term] = userStake` happens at the end. If the user is a malicious contract, the `CreditToken.transfer` callback can reenter `getRewards` for the same user/term. Since `_stakes[user][term]` hasn't been updated yet, the reentrant call sees the old `profitIndex` and can claim the same rewards again, or reenter `unstake` to withdraw the stake while rewards are being computed.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker stakes CREDIT via `stake`. 2) Attacker calls `getRewards` (or triggers it via `unstake`/`updateMintRatio`). 3) During the `CreditToken.transfer(user, creditReward)` callback, the attacker reenters `getRewards` for the same user/term. 4) The reentrant call sees the stale `userStake.profitIndex` and computes the same `creditReward` again, transferring double rewards.
hypotheses.impact: Double-claiming of CREDIT and GUILD rewards, draining the ProfitManager and RateLimitedMinter buffers.
hypotheses.recommendation: Update `_stakes[user][term]` before transferring rewards, and add a `nonReentrant` modifier to `getRewards`, `stake`, `unstake`, and `updateMintRatio`.

hypotheses.title: LendingTermOffboarding poll can be griefed to block offboarding
hypotheses.description: `proposeOffboard` requires `block.number > lastPollBlock[term] + POLL_DURATION_BLOCKS`. An attacker can call `proposeOffboard(term)` with minimal cost (just gas, no GUILD needed) to create a poll with 1 wei of voting power, then never support it. This sets `lastPollBlock[term]` to the current block, blocking any new offboarding poll for that term for `POLL_DURATION_BLOCKS` (~7 days). The attacker can repeat this every 7 days to permanently prevent offboarding of a malicious or failing term.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker calls `proposeOffboard(term)` — succeeds with 1 wei voting power. 2) No one supports the poll; it expires after 7 days. 3) Attacker calls `proposeOffboard(term)` again immediately after expiry. 4) Repeat indefinitely. 5) Legitimate GUILD holders can never create a poll to offboard the term.
hypotheses.impact: Offboarding mechanism permanently blocked for a term; bad debt cannot be stopped; GUILD holders lose the ability to remove a failing term.
hypotheses.recommendation: Require a minimum GUILD weight to create a poll, or allow multiple concurrent polls per term.

hypotheses.title: LendingTermOffboarding.offboard and cleanup are permissionless
hypotheses.description: `offboard()` and `cleanup()` have no access control beyond `whenNotPaused` and the `canOffboard[term]` flag. Once quorum is reached, ANY external caller can trigger `offboard`, which removes the gauge and pauses PSM redemptions. `cleanup` similarly can be called by anyone once `issuance == 0` and the gauge is deprecated. While the quorum gate is intended, the lack of a designated caller means an attacker can front-run legitimate offboarding/cleanup calls, or trigger cleanup at a moment that is unfavorable (e.g., immediately after the last loan closes, before governance can review).
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker monitors `canOffboard[term]` becoming true. 2) Attacker calls `offboard(term)` immediately, removing the gauge and pausing PSM redemptions. 3) Later, attacker calls `cleanup(term)` as soon as `issuance == 0`, revoking roles and unpausing PSM.
hypotheses.impact: Attacker controls timing of offboarding and cleanup, potentially causing denial of service for borrowers trying to repay, or forcing PSM redemptions to be paused/unpaused at attacker-chosen times. In the worst case, cleanup can be called before all loans are properly settled if `issuance` accounting is off.
hypotheses.recommendation: Restrict `offboard` and `cleanup` to a trusted role (e.g., GOVERNOR or a dedicated keeper role), or at minimum require the caller to be the one who reached quorum.

hypotheses.title: SurplusGuildMinter.updateMintRatio is permissionless and can grief users
hypotheses.description: `updateMintRatio(address user, address term)` is external with no access control. It calls `getRewards(user, term)` which applies pending rewards and can slash the user if a gauge loss occurred. Then it updates the user's guild stake based on the current `mintRatio`. An attacker can call this for any user at any time, forcing reward realization and stake updates. While `getRewards` is idempotent, the forced update can be used to grief users by triggering slashing at an inopportune moment, or by forcing a stake reduction when `mintRatio` has decreased.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker monitors `mintRatio` changes or gauge losses. 2) Attacker calls `updateMintRatio(victim, term)` for a victim. 3) If a loss occurred, the victim is slashed immediately; if `mintRatio` decreased, the victim's guild stake is reduced and burned.
hypotheses.impact: Griefing: victims lose guild rewards or are slashed at attacker-chosen times. While the economic outcome may be the same eventually, the timing can be manipulated for MEV or to force losses before a user can react.
hypotheses.recommendation: Restrict `updateMintRatio` to the user themselves (i.e., `msg.sender == user`) or to a trusted role.

hypotheses.title: onBid uses stale creditMultiplier for principal, mis-accounting PnL
hypotheses.description: In `onBid`, `principal` is recomputed as `borrowAmount * borrowCreditMultiplier / creditMultiplier` using the *current* `creditMultiplier`. But `callDebt` (the amount the auction is trying to recover) was fixed at call time using the multiplier at that moment. If `creditMultiplier` drops between call and bid (e.g. another term reports a loss), the recomputed `principal` is larger than the principal implied by `callDebt`, so `interest = creditFromBidder - principal` can be negative even when the bidder paid more than the original principal, and `pnl` is misreported. Conversely, if the multiplier rises (it can't, but the reverse case matters for the loss branch), the loss branch sets `principal = creditFromBidder` and requires `collateralToBorrower == 0`, which may not hold.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker calls a loan in term A. 2) Before anyone bids, attacker triggers a loss in term B (via a separate loan) that lowers `creditMultiplier`. 3) Attacker bids on the auction in term A. 4) `principal` is recomputed with the new lower multiplier, inflating it relative to `callDebt`. 5) The `pnl` reported to ProfitManager is wrong (loss reported where there was profit, or vice versa), and `issuance -= borrowAmount` uses the original `borrowAmount` while the actual debt recovered differs.
hypotheses.impact: Wrong PnL reporting to ProfitManager, potentially burning surplus buffer or lowering `creditMultiplier` unnecessarily, and mis-stating `issuance`. Repeated across auctions this can drain the surplus buffer or unfairly slash CREDIT holders.
hypotheses.recommendation: Store the principal (or the creditMultiplier at call time) in the Loan struct when `_call` is invoked, and use that stored value in `onBid` instead of recomputing with the current multiplier.

hypotheses.title: LendingTerm._borrow uses creditMultiplier before it can change, but maxBorrow ignores interest/openingFee
hypotheses.description: `maxBorrow = collateralAmount * maxDebtPerCollateralToken / creditMultiplier` only bounds the principal, not the total debt including openingFee and accrued interest. A borrower can borrow up to the max, immediately owe more than maxBorrow due to openingFee, and the loan is undercollateralized from block one. Since the term has no liquidation-by-price mechanism (only call on missed partial repay or offboarding), the protocol relies on the auction to recover, but the auction starts from an already-underwater position.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker picks a term with openingFee > 0. 2) Borrows exactly maxBorrow. 3) Immediately the loan debt = maxBorrow * (1 + openingFee) > maxBorrow, exceeding the collateral's max debt capacity. 4) Attacker defaults (never repays), forcing an auction that cannot recover full debt even at full collateral value.
hypotheses.impact: Systematic undercollateralization; bad debt accrues to surplus buffer / credit holders on every borrow at the cap.
hypotheses.recommendation: Include openingFee (and a conservative interest buffer) in the maxBorrow check, e.g. require borrowAmount * (1e18 + openingFee) / 1e18 <= maxBorrow.

hypotheses.title: Reentrancy in LendingTerm._partialRepay via CreditToken hooks
hypotheses.description: `_partialRepay` updates `loans[loanId].borrowAmount`, `lastPartialRepay`, and `issuance` before calling `CreditToken.transferFrom`, `CreditToken.transfer`, `CreditToken.burn`, and `RateLimitedMinter.replenishBuffer`. CreditToken is an ERC20RebaseDistributor with complex transfer logic that can call back into the LendingTerm if the repayer is a contract. A malicious repayer contract can reenter `_partialRepay` for the same loanId (the `borrowTime < block.timestamp` check passes since the loan was opened in a prior block) and repay again, or reenter `_repay` to close the loan, or reenter `_borrow` to open a new loan. The state updates in `_partialRepay` are done before the external calls, but the reentrant call sees the partially-updated state and can exploit the `issuance` decrement.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker deploys a contract that calls `partialRepay` and reenters on the CreditToken transfer callback. 2) The reentrant call can call `_repay` on the same loanId, which would pass the `closeTime == 0` check (since `_partialRepay` doesn't set closeTime) and repay the remaining debt. 3) Alternatively, reenter `_borrow` to open a new loan while `issuance` is temporarily reduced.
hypotheses.impact: Double-repayment accounting errors, issuance manipulation, and potential loss of funds for the protocol or other users.
hypotheses.recommendation: Add a `nonReentrant` modifier to `partialRepay`, `repay`, `borrow`, `addCollateral`, and `call`, and ensure all state updates precede external calls.

hypotheses.title: callMany can be griefed to exceed block gas limit
hypotheses.description: `callMany(bytes32[] memory loanIds)` loops over a caller-supplied array and calls `_call` for each, which calls `AuctionHouse.startAuction` and writes storage. There is no cap on array length. A caller can pass an arbitrarily large array, but more importantly, an attacker can front-run or grief by making the array large enough that the transaction exceeds the block gas limit, causing the entire batch to revert. Since `callMany` is the only batch mechanism, users relying on it to call many loans (e.g., after a term is deprecated) can be blocked.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Term is deprecated, many loans need to be called. 2) Attacker submits `callMany` with a huge array (or the natural array is large). 3) Transaction reverts due to out-of-gas. 4) No loans get called in that batch; users must call individually, but if any single loan's `_call` reverts (e.g., due to a reverting collateral token), the whole batch is blocked.
hypotheses.impact: Loans cannot be called in batch, delaying auctions and potentially causing bad debt to accumulate. Griefing vector for blocking liquidation.
hypotheses.recommendation: Add a maximum batch size parameter, or make `callMany` skip reverting entries instead of reverting the whole batch.

hypotheses.title: LendingTerm loanId collision allows overwriting loan state
hypotheses.description: `loanId = keccak256(abi.encode(borrower, address(this), block.timestamp))`. Two loans opened by the same borrower in the same block (via a contract calling borrow twice, or via a multicall) will produce the same loanId. The check `require(loans[loanId].borrowTime == 0)` prevents overwriting, but the second borrow reverts. However, if a borrower opens a loan, repays it in the same block (closeTime set), then opens another loan in the same block, the loanId is identical and `borrowTime != 0` so the second borrow reverts — this is a DoS on the borrower, not a theft. More critically, the loanId does not include a nonce, so a borrower cannot open two loans in the same block even with different collateral/amounts. This is a usability/DoS issue, not a signature replay.
hypotheses.attackPath: A borrower using a smart contract that opens two loans in one transaction (e.g., for different collateral) will have the second call revert due to loanId collision. An attacker cannot exploit this to steal funds, only to grief.
hypotheses.impact: DoS on legitimate borrowers opening multiple loans in the same block.
hypotheses.recommendation: Include a nonce or the borrowAmount/collateralAmount in the loanId hash.

hypotheses.title: SimplePSM.mintAndEnterRebase can be used to capture rebase rewards unfairly
hypotheses.description: `mintAndEnterRebase` mints CREDIT and immediately enters rebase. If a distribution is pending (interpolation in progress), the new rebaser's shares are computed at the current share price, which already includes the interpolated portion of the distribution. This means the new rebaser captures a share of the ongoing distribution without having held CREDIT during the distribution event. An attacker can monitor for `distribute` calls and immediately call `mintAndEnterRebase` to capture a share of the rewards.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker observes `CreditToken.distribute` call (via ProfitManager profit). 2) Attacker calls `SimplePSM.mintAndEnterRebase` with a large amount. 3) Attacker's shares are computed at the current share price (which is interpolating upward). 4) Attacker captures a share of the remaining distribution. 5) Attacker exits rebase after interpolation, receiving rewards.
hypotheses.impact: Long-term CREDIT holders receive diluted rewards; attacker extracts value from the savings rate.
hypotheses.recommendation: Snapshot rebasing supply at distribution time, or require a minimum holding period before rewards are claimable.

hypotheses.title: LendingTerm._partialRepay uses unchecked transferFrom return
hypotheses.description: `CreditToken(refs.creditToken).transferFrom(repayer, address(this), debtToRepay)` is called without checking the return value. CreditToken inherits from ERC20RebaseDistributor which overrides transferFrom and returns a bool. If the transfer silently returns false (e.g., due to a rebasing edge case or a future token upgrade), the loan state is already updated (borrowAmount decreased, issuance decreased, lastPartialRepay set) but no CREDIT was actually pulled. The same pattern appears in `_repay` and `onBid`.
hypotheses.attackPath: If CreditToken.transferFrom ever returns false without reverting (e.g., a rebasing accounting edge case where the sender's balance is insufficient after rebase materialization), the borrower gets their debt reduced without paying. Repeated calls drain the protocol's accounting.
hypotheses.impact: Debt is reduced without payment; issuance accounting diverges from actual CREDIT supply; protocol insolvency.
hypotheses.recommendation: Use SafeERC20.safeTransferFrom for CreditToken transfers, or wrap with `require(...transferFrom(...), "...")`.

hypotheses.title: SurplusGuildMinter.unstake uses stale mintRatio for partial unstake
hypotheses.description: `unstake` computes `userMintRatio = userStake.guild * 1e18 / userStake.credit` and then `guildAmount = userMintRatio * amount / 1e18`. This is correct only if the user's stake was minted at a single ratio. But `updateMintRatio` can change a user's `guild` balance without changing `credit`, and `mintRatio` can be changed by governance between stake and unstake. If a user stakes at ratio R1, then `updateMintRatio` is called after governance sets ratio R2, the user's `guild` reflects a blend. The derived `userMintRatio` is then used to burn GUILD on partial unstake, which can burn more or fewer GUILD than the proportional share, leaving the remaining stake's `guild/credit` ratio inconsistent with the current `mintRatio`.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker stakes at ratio R1. 2) Governance changes `mintRatio` to R2 (or attacker calls `updateMintRatio` after such a change). 3) Attacker partially unstakes. 4) The derived `userMintRatio` may be higher than R2, so the attacker burns fewer GUILD than the CREDIT withdrawn proportionally warrants, or vice versa. 5) Attacker repeats to extract value from the GUILD mint/burn spread.
hypotheses.impact: GUILD supply accounting drifts from CREDIT staked; attackers can extract GUILD (mint more than burn) or grief other stakers by burning disproportionate GUILD. The `RateLimitedMinter` buffer is also mis-replenished.
hypotheses.recommendation: On partial unstake, burn GUILD proportional to the current `mintRatio` (or store the ratio at stake time per user), and reconcile any delta against the user's stored `guild` balance.

hypotheses.title: SimplePSM.getMintAmountOut uses live creditMultiplier, enabling PSM arbitrage on multiplier drops
hypotheses.description: The PSM mints CREDIT at `amountIn * decimalCorrection * 1e18 / creditMultiplier`. When creditMultiplier drops (bad debt), the PSM mints more CREDIT per peg token, but the redeemableCredit() used in ProfitManager.totalBorrowedCredit() also scales. An attacker who front-runs the multiplier update (or observes the loss transaction in the mempool) can mint CREDIT at the old rate and redeem after the drop, or vice versa, extracting value from the PSM's pegTokenBalance.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker sees a pending loss notification that will lower creditMultiplier. 2) Before it lands, attacker redeems CREDIT for peg tokens at the higher multiplier (getRedeemAmountOut uses current multiplier). 3) After the drop, attacker mints CREDIT back at the lower multiplier, receiving more CREDIT for the same peg tokens. 4) Net profit in CREDIT, diluting other holders.
hypotheses.impact: Value extraction from PSM reserves; CREDIT holders diluted; peg destabilized.
hypotheses.recommendation: This is inherent to a PSM tied to a mutable multiplier; consider pausing PSM mint/redeem around multiplier updates, or using a time-weighted multiplier.

hypotheses.title: ProfitManager.notifyPnL creditMultiplier update uses totalSupply including unminted rebase rewards
hypotheses.description: When a loss exceeds the surplus buffer, `newCreditMultiplier = creditMultiplier * (creditTotalSupply - loss) / creditTotalSupply` where `creditTotalSupply = CreditToken.totalSupply()`. CreditToken.totalSupply() includes `unmintedRebaseRewards()` (interpolated pending rewards). These unminted rewards are not yet real balances and will be minted later, so subtracting `loss` from a supply that includes them understates the multiplier reduction, leaving CREDIT overvalued relative to the actual loss. Conversely, the loss burn reduces real supply but the denominator includes phantom supply.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) A loss occurs while a large rebase distribution is mid-interpolation (unmintedRebaseRewards > 0). 2) notifyPnL computes newCreditMultiplier using inflated totalSupply. 3) The multiplier is reduced less than it should be. 4) CREDIT holders (including the attacker who entered rebase) redeem at the PSM for more peg tokens than the true post-loss value.
hypotheses.impact: CREDIT holders extract more peg tokens than warranted; PSM reserves depleted; remaining holders diluted.
hypotheses.recommendation: Use ERC20.totalSupply() (raw) or targetTotalSupply() consistently, and account for unminted rebase rewards explicitly when computing the multiplier.

hypotheses.title: Read-only reentrancy in ProfitManager.notifyPnL via CreditToken.distribute
hypotheses.description: In `notifyPnL`, when `amount > 0`, the function calls `CreditToken(_credit).distribute(amountForCredit)` which burns tokens from the ProfitManager and updates the rebasing share price interpolation. The `distribute` function calls `_burn` on the CreditToken, which can trigger `_decrementVotesUntilFree` and other hooks. If a malicious contract is the `otherRecipient` (set by governance, but the recipient itself is untrusted), the `CreditToken.transfer` to `otherRecipient` happens before `distribute` and before the gauge profit index update. A malicious `otherRecipient` can reenter `notifyPnL` or read stale `gaugeProfitIndex` values during the callback, or reenter `claimGaugeRewards` to claim rewards based on a stale index.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker is set as `otherRecipient` (or controls a contract that is). 2) When `notifyPnL` is called with a profit, the `CreditToken.transfer` to `otherRecipient` triggers the attacker's fallback. 3) The attacker reenters `ProfitManager.claimGaugeRewards` or `getPendingRewards` to read the stale `gaugeProfitIndex` before it's updated, or reenters `notifyPnL` to double-count profits.
hypotheses.impact: Incorrect reward distribution, double-claiming of gauge rewards, and manipulation of the profit index.
hypotheses.recommendation: Update `gaugeProfitIndex` and all state before making external calls, and add a reentrancy guard to `notifyPnL` and `claimGaugeRewards`.

hypotheses.title: SurplusGuildMinter unstake blocked by withdrawFromTermSurplusBuffer role
hypotheses.description: `unstake()` calls `ProfitManager(profitManager).withdrawFromTermSurplusBuffer(term, msg.sender, amount)`, which is restricted to `CoreRoles.GUILD_SURPLUS_BUFFER_WITHDRAW`. The SurplusGuildMinter contract must hold this role. If governance revokes this role from SurplusGuildMinter (e.g., during a migration or as a precaution), all users' `unstake()` calls revert, trapping their staked CREDIT in the term surplus buffer. There is no alternative withdrawal path for users.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Governance revokes `GUILD_SURPLUS_BUFFER_WITHDRAW` from SurplusGuildMinter (trusted action, but the impact is on untrusted users). 2) Users call `unstake()` — reverts. 3) Staked CREDIT is stuck in ProfitManager's `termSurplusBuffer`. 4) Users cannot recover funds.
hypotheses.impact: User funds frozen in term surplus buffer; no user-accessible recovery path.
hypotheses.recommendation: Add a fallback withdrawal path or ensure the role cannot be revoked while stakes exist.

hypotheses.title: LendingTermOffboarding.cleanup can be called before offboard
hypotheses.description: `cleanup` requires `canOffboard[term]` and `GuildToken(guildToken).isDeprecatedGauge(term)`. However, `canOffboard[term]` is set to true as soon as quorum is reached in `supportOffboard`, before `offboard()` is called. If a term is deprecated through another path (e.g., governance directly calls `removeGauge`), `isDeprecatedGauge` returns true while `nOffboardingsInProgress` was never incremented. Then `cleanup` executes `--nOffboardingsInProgress`, which underflows and reverts (or if it doesn't revert due to unchecked, corrupts the counter). Since Solidity 0.8.x, this reverts, but the term cannot be cleaned up.
hypotheses.attackPath: Governance (trusted) is out of scope, but any user can call `cleanup` after quorum is reached and the term is deprecated by any means. If `offboard()` was never called (e.g., term deprecated via direct governance action), `nOffboardingsInProgress` is 0 and `--nOffboardingsInProgress` underflows, reverting cleanup permanently.
hypotheses.impact: Term roles cannot be revoked; PSM redemptions may stay paused; term stuck in limbo.
hypotheses.recommendation: Track offboarding state per-term (e.g., a mapping) rather than relying on a global counter, or require that `offboard()` was called before `cleanup()`.

hypotheses.title: LendingTerm.forgive sets hardCap to 0 but does not revoke roles
hypotheses.description: `forgive()` is restricted to GOVERNOR, but it sets `params.hardCap = 0` to prevent new borrows. However, it does NOT revoke the `RATE_LIMITED_CREDIT_MINTER` or `GAUGE_PNL_NOTIFIER` roles from the term, nor does it remove the gauge. This means the term can still be used for other operations (e.g., `onBid` callbacks, `partialRepay`, `repay`), and the gauge weight remains. If governance forgets to offboard the term, the term remains in a half-broken state where `hardCap == 0` but the gauge is still active, potentially allowing `debtCeiling` calculations to return non-zero and confusing other contracts.
hypotheses.attackPath: Not directly exploitable by an untrusted actor, but a malicious borrower could exploit the half-broken state: after `forgive`, the loan is closed but the term still has roles. If a new loan could somehow be opened (it can't due to hardCap == 0), or if `onBid` is called on a stale loan, accounting could be corrupted.
hypotheses.impact: Inconsistent state: term is not fully offboarded, gauge weight remains, roles remain. Could lead to accounting errors if governance does not follow up with offboarding.
hypotheses.recommendation: In `forgive`, also revoke the term's roles and remove the gauge, or require that the term is already offboarded before forgiving.

hypotheses.title: ProfitManager.claimGaugeRewards is permissionless and can be used to grief
hypotheses.description: `claimGaugeRewards(address user, address gauge)` is public and permissionless. It transfers pending CREDIT rewards to `user`. While this is generally benign (the user gets their rewards), it can be used to grief users by forcing reward realization at a moment when the user would prefer to keep rewards unclaimed (e.g., to avoid triggering a taxable event, or to keep the profit index unchanged for a subsequent operation). More importantly, it can be called in a loop to force many small transfers, potentially causing gas griefing for the user's future transactions.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker calls `claimGaugeRewards(victim, gauge)` repeatedly. 2) Each call transfers a small amount of CREDIT to the victim, updating `userGaugeProfitIndex`. 3) The victim's future transactions may be more expensive due to the updated state, or the victim may be forced to realize rewards.
hypotheses.impact: Minor griefing: forced reward realization, potential gas cost increase for the victim. No direct loss of funds.
hypotheses.recommendation: Restrict `claimGaugeRewards` to `msg.sender == user` or to a trusted role, or document that it is intentionally permissionless.

hypotheses.title: SimplePSM.redeemableCredit uses current multiplier, enabling PSM arbitrage on multiplier drop
hypotheses.description: `redeemableCredit()` returns `getMintAmountOut(pegTokenBalance)`, which uses the *current* `creditMultiplier`. `ProfitManager.totalBorrowedCredit()` subtracts `redeemableCredit()` from `targetTotalSupply()`. When `creditMultiplier` drops (bad debt), `redeemableCredit()` increases (more CREDIT mintable per peg token), so `totalBorrowedCredit()` decreases. This is intended, but it means a user can mint CREDIT at the new (cheaper) rate and redeem at the old rate if they act before the multiplier update propagates, or vice versa. More concretely, a user can front-run a known multiplier drop by redeeming CREDIT for peg tokens at the pre-drop rate, then re-mint after the drop at the post-drop rate, extracting the difference from the PSM's peg token balance.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker holds CREDIT. 2) Attacker anticipates a multiplier drop (e.g. a large loan about to be forgiven or a loss notified). 3) Attacker redeems CREDIT for peg tokens at the pre-drop rate. 4) Multiplier drops. 5) Attacker mints CREDIT with the same peg tokens at the post-drop rate, receiving more CREDIT. 6) Attacker repeats or holds the extra CREDIT. The PSM's `pegTokenBalance` is drained of value.
hypotheses.impact: PSM peg token reserves are arbitraged; CREDIT holders and the protocol lose the difference. If repeated, the PSM can be drained, breaking the peg guarantee.
hypotheses.recommendation: Pause redemptions during multiplier updates, or use a time-weighted multiplier for PSM mint/redeem, or require a cooldown between mint and redeem.

hypotheses.title: AuctionHouse.getBidDetail first-phase collateral rounds down to zero early
hypotheses.description: In the first phase, `collateralReceived = collateralAmount * elapsed / midPoint`. For small `collateralAmount` or early `elapsed`, this rounds down to 0. A bidder calling `bid` at that point would receive 0 collateral while paying the full `callDebt`, and `onBid` would then require `collateralOut == collateralAmount || collateralOut == 0`. Since `collateralToBidder == 0` and `collateralToBorrower == collateralAmount`, the check passes, but the bidder paid full debt for zero collateral. This is a griefing/self-harm vector, but more importantly it means the auction can be "won" by a bidder who pays full debt and receives nothing, which is economically irrational but possible if the bidder is the borrower themselves trying to close the loan cheaply (they get collateral back as `collateralToBorrower`).
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Borrower's loan is called. 2) Borrower immediately calls `bid` in the first block of the auction. 3) `collateralReceived` rounds to 0, so `collateralToBorrower = collateralAmount` and `collateralToBidder = 0`. 4) Borrower pays `callDebt` in CREDIT but receives all collateral back. 5) Borrower effectively repays the loan at the call-debt price without losing collateral, which is the intended behavior of `repay`, but here it bypasses the `repay` path's interest accounting (interest is computed differently in `onBid`).
hypotheses.impact: Minor accounting discrepancy between `repay` and `bid` paths; borrower can choose the cheaper path. Not a direct loss of funds but a consistency issue in interest/PnL accounting.
hypotheses.recommendation: Require `collateralReceived != 0` in `bid`, or start the first phase with a minimum elapsed time so collateral is non-zero.

hypotheses.title: LendingTerm.getLoanDebt interest accrual uses block.timestamp without cap, allowing interest overflow on long-lived loans
hypotheses.description: `interest = borrowAmount * interestRate * (block.timestamp - borrowTime) / YEAR / 1e18`. For very long-lived loans (years) with high interestRate, the multiplication can approach overflow, but more practically the linear (non-compounding) interest means the debt grows unboundedly relative to collateral, and there is no cap. Combined with the fact that call() only triggers on missed partial repay or offboarding, a loan can sit for years accruing interest far exceeding collateral value, guaranteeing bad debt at auction.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker opens a loan with maxDelayBetweenPartialRepay = 0 (no periodic repay) on a term that is not offboarded. 2) Attacker never repays. 3) Interest accrues linearly forever; collateral value is fixed. 4) When eventually called, auction cannot recover the inflated debt.
hypotheses.impact: Guaranteed bad debt on any long-lived loan; surplus buffer / credit holders absorb losses.
hypotheses.recommendation: Cap accrued interest or require periodic partial repayments (maxDelayBetweenPartialRepay != 0) for all terms, or add a health check that calls loans when debt exceeds collateral capacity.

hypotheses.title: LendingTerm._borrow loanId collision within same block
hypotheses.description: `loanId = keccak256(abi.encode(borrower, address(this), block.timestamp))`. If the same borrower opens two loans in the same block (e.g., via a contract calling borrow twice, or via a multicall), the second call reverts with "loan exists". This is a griefing/DoS vector: an attacker can front-run a victim's borrow in the same block by calling borrow with the same parameters? No — the borrower is msg.sender, so only the borrower themselves can collide. However, a borrower using a smart contract that batches borrows will be unable to open multiple loans in one block, and more critically, if a borrower's transaction is included in the same block as a prior borrow by the same address (e.g., via a relayer or account abstraction), it reverts.
hypotheses.attackPath: A borrower using a smart contract wallet or batching mechanism cannot open two loans in the same block. More subtly, if a borrower's first borrow tx is included and they retry in the same block, it reverts. Not directly exploitable by an untrusted third party.
hypotheses.impact: Legitimate borrowers cannot open multiple loans in one block; potential DoS for batched operations.
hypotheses.recommendation: Include a nonce or a counter in the loanId derivation to allow multiple loans per block per borrower.

hypotheses.title: AuctionHouse.bid allows bidder to be the LendingTerm itself
hypotheses.description: `bid` calls `LendingTerm(_lendingTerm).onBid(loanId, msg.sender, ...)`. If `msg.sender` is the LendingTerm contract itself (or another contract that has been granted the RATE_LIMITED_CREDIT_MINTER role), the CREDIT transferFrom in onBid would pull from the term's own balance. More importantly, `onBid` does `CreditToken(refs.creditToken).transferFrom(bidder, address(this), creditFromBidder)`. If bidder is a contract without CREDIT approval, it reverts. No direct exploit, but the assumption that bidder is an EOA or approved contract is not enforced.
hypotheses.attackPath: Not directly exploitable by an untrusted actor without CREDIT approval. Low severity.
hypotheses.impact: No concrete damage identified.
hypotheses.recommendation: No change needed; document the assumption.

hypotheses.title: delegateBySig allows signature replay via missing signer-zero check ordering
hypotheses.description: The function calls `_useNonce(signer)` before verifying `signer != address(0)`. If `ecrecover` returns address(0) (invalid signature), `_useNonce(address(0))` is consumed and then the require on signer fails, but more importantly the nonce check is performed against the recovered signer without first ensuring the signature is valid. Combined with the fact that `_delegate` is called with the recovered signer, an attacker who can obtain any valid signature over the DELEGATION_TYPEHASH payload can replay it on any chain where this contract is deployed at the same address, since the domain separator includes chainId but the contract does not enforce a per-deployment salt beyond the standard EIP-712 domain. The bigger issue: the nonce is consumed from `signer`'s nonce mapping, but the check `nonce == _useNonce(signer)` happens after ecrecover, so a malleable signature (flipping s and v) produces a different but valid signature that still recovers the same signer and consumes the same nonce — however since nonce is consumed, replay is prevented. The real flaw is that `_useNonce` is called on the recovered signer before the zero-address check, allowing griefing of address(0)'s nonce, and more critically the ordering means an invalid signature still mutates state.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker crafts a signature with v/r/s that ecrecover resolves to address(0). 2) Calls delegateBySig with that signature. 3) `_useNonce(address(0))` is executed, incrementing address(0)'s nonce. 4) The require(signer != address(0)) reverts, but the nonce increment is rolled back with the revert — so no actual state change. The actual exploitable path: if a user signs a delegation with a nonce, and the same signed message is valid on a forked chain or a chain where the contract is deployed at the same address with the same domain separator (chainId is in domain, so cross-chain is mitigated), replay is prevented by nonce. However, the missing check is that `signer != address(0)` should be before `_useNonce`. This is a low-severity ordering issue.
hypotheses.impact: Nonce griefing on address(0) is reverted, so no real impact. The finding is weak.
hypotheses.recommendation: Move `require(signer != address(0))` before `_useNonce(signer)`.
